facts.text: Surveyor 3 launched on 17 April 1967. Unlike earlier Surveyors it began its trip from a parking orbit around Earth, with a burn from a Centaur upper stage that could now fire more than once.
Surveyor 3 was the third engineering flight of the series, but for the first time carried a surface-sampling instrument that could reach up to 1.5 m from the lander and dig up to 18 cm deep.

During descent, highly reflective rocks confused the radar and the main engine did not cut off at about 4.3 m. Surveyor 3 bounced twice, first to 10 m and then to 3 m, and the third time it settled into a soft landing.
Surveyor 3 landed at 00:04:17 UT on 20 April 1967 in the southeastern Oceanus Procellarum, at 3 degrees south, 23.41 degrees west.
Less than an hour after landing it began transmitting the first of 6,326 TV pictures of its surroundings.
The TV camera had two lenses, 25 and 100 mm, under a mirror that could move left, right, up and down. A 200-line picture took about 20 seconds to send.
On commands from Earth the sampler dug four trenches and made four bearing tests and thirteen impact tests.
The tests showed lunar soil is like wet sand, with a bearing strength of about 0.7 kg per square centimetre: solid enough to support an Apollo Lunar Module.
The last contact with Surveyor 3 was on 4 May 1967, two days after the lunar night began.
More than two years later, Apollo 12 astronauts Charles Conrad and Alan Bean landed the Intrepid Lunar Module about 180 m from the inactive Surveyor 3.
On their second moonwalk the astronauts walked over to Surveyor 3 and recovered parts, including the soil scoop and camera system, to study the effects of nearly two and a half years on the Moon.
